questions.question: What is the difference between a defining and a non-defining relative clause?
options: A defining clause gives necessary information (no comma); a non-defining clause adds extra information (with commas)
A defining clause always comes first in the sentence
A non-defining clause gives necessary information; a defining clause is extra
They are identical in writing
questions.explanation: Defining clauses are essential to identify who or what we mean and take no comma. Non-defining clauses add extra information and are set off with commas.

questions.question: In which type of relative clause can you use "that"?
options: Only in defining relative clauses
Only in non-defining relative clauses
In both types
In neither type
questions.explanation: "That" can replace who/which in defining clauses ("the book that I read"), but NOT in non-defining clauses with commas.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: My sister, who lives in London, is a doctor.
My sister who lives in London, is a doctor.
My sister, that lives in London, is a doctor.
My sister which lives in London is a doctor.
questions.explanation: This non-defining clause adds extra information, so it needs commas and "who" (not "that"). "Which" is used for things, not people.

questions.question: What is a simple test to decide if a relative clause is non-defining?
options: Remove the clause - if the sentence still makes full sense, it is non-defining
Count the words in the clause
Check if the clause contains a verb
See if the sentence starts with "The"
questions.explanation: If you can remove the clause and the sentence still makes full sense, the clause is non-defining and needs commas.

questions.question: Which conjunction introduces a concession clause (innrømming)?
options: Although
Because
So that
When
questions.explanation: "Although" introduces a concession ("Although it rained, we went out"). "Because" gives a reason, "so that" a purpose, and "when" a time.
